description: Roles of jurors, witnesses, magistrates and special constables, and how citizens can change the law.
content_html:
Citizens as Active Participants in the Legal System

The UK’s legal system does not function through paid professionals alone. Ordinary citizens play essential roles in delivering justice — from serving on juries to sitting as magistrates, from volunteering as special constables to standing as police and crime commissioners. Understanding these roles shows how the legal system is, in part, a civic institution that depends on public participation.

The Role of the Juror

A juror is a citizen selected at random from the electoral register to serve on a jury in a Crown Court trial. Jury service is a legal obligation — most adults on the electoral register between the ages of 18 and 75 are eligible to be called and must attend unless they have a valid reason to be excused. The jury of twelve hears evidence presented by both the prosecution and the defence, and then deliberates in private to reach a verdict of guilty or not guilty.

The jury system is a cornerstone of the English legal tradition. Supporters argue it reflects the principle that a defendant should be judged by peers from their own community rather than solely by legal professionals, and that it brings common sense and public values into the courtroom. Critics argue that jurors may be swayed by emotion, lack the legal expertise to evaluate complex evidence, and that trials by jury are lengthy and expensive. Jury trials are used only for the most serious criminal offences in the Crown Court; the majority of criminal cases are decided by magistrates.

Supporters argue: The jury embodies the principle that justice belongs to the community, not just the state. Having twelve citizens deliberate independently reduces the risk of arbitrary or biased decisions by a single judge. Historically, juries have acquitted defendants when public opinion judged the law itself to be unjust. In high-profile cases, a jury verdict carries a democratic legitimacy that a professional judge’s ruling alone may not.

Critics argue: Jurors have no legal training and may struggle to understand complex financial or scientific evidence. Cases can be influenced by media coverage or jurors’ unconscious biases. Jury trials are significantly more expensive and time-consuming than magistrates’ court proceedings, adding to court backlogs. Some argue that for many serious cases, a single experienced judge or a panel of judges would produce more consistent verdicts.

The Role of Witnesses

A witness may be called to give evidence in both criminal and civil cases. Witnesses are required to tell the truth — giving false testimony is the criminal offence of perjury. Victims of crime also play a role as witnesses for the prosecution; their witness statements and, in many cases, their live testimony form part of the evidence the jury or magistrates consider. Witness support services exist to help vulnerable witnesses, including children and victims of serious offences, to give evidence in less intimidating ways (for example, via video link or behind a screen).

Magistrates

A magistrate (also known as a Justice of the Peace, or JP) is a volunteer citizen who sits on the magistrates’ court bench. Unlike professional judges, magistrates are not legally trained: they are advised on points of law by a legally qualified court adviser (formerly called a clerk). Magistrates typically sit in panels of three and hear approximately 95% of all criminal cases in England and Wales — mainly less serious offences such as motoring offences, minor theft, low-level assault and public order offences.

To become a magistrate, a person must apply to the Judicial Appointments Commission and be assessed for qualities including good character, social awareness, sound judgement and the ability to see things from another’s perspective. Magistrates commit to sitting for a minimum of 26 half-days per year. There is a drive to recruit magistrates who reflect the diversity of the communities they serve. Magistrates can impose fines, community orders and short custodial sentences; for more serious cases, they can commit defendants to the Crown Court for sentencing.

Key Fact

Magistrates (Justices of the Peace) are unpaid volunteers who hear approximately 95% of all criminal cases in England and Wales. They are advised by a legally qualified court adviser and typically sit in panels of three.

Special Constables

A special constable is a volunteer who carries out policing duties alongside regular officers. Special constables have the same powers of arrest, search and detention as a regular police constable. They undergo training before deployment and commit to a minimum number of hours of duty each month. Special constables contribute to visible policing, community engagement and operational support, particularly during major events or periods of high demand.

Police and Crime Commissioners

A Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) is directly elected by voters in each police force area in England and Wales. PCCs set the local police and crime plan, determine the police budget, appoint or dismiss the chief constable and are accountable to the public through elections. The PCC role was created in 2012 to make local policing more directly accountable to the communities it serves. PCCs are not operational police officers; they hold the force to account rather than directing day-to-day policing.

Members of Tribunal Hearings

Tribunals are specialist judicial bodies that deal with disputes outside the ordinary court system. A tribunal typically consists of a legally qualified judge and two lay members (citizens with expertise in the relevant field, not legal professionals). Employment tribunals hear claims about unfair dismissal, discrimination and equal pay. Immigration tribunals hear appeals against asylum and visa decisions. Lay members bring practical knowledge of the relevant sector to supplement the judge’s legal expertise.

How Citizens Can Bring About Legal Change

Citizens are not passive subjects of the law — they can actively work to change it. Forms of democratic and citizenship action include joining an interest group or pressure group that campaigns for legal reform, signing or organising petitions, contacting MPs or local councillors, lobbying government departments, joining or organising peaceful demonstrations, using the media to publicise an injustice, and bringing a legal challenge (such as a judicial review) if a public authority has acted unlawfully.

Key Fact

Historical examples of citizens successfully campaigning for legal change include the Hillsborough families (campaigning for a new inquest and changes to police accountability law), and Stephen Lawrence’s family (whose campaign led to the Macpherson Report and changes to the Race Relations Act).

Pressure groups, charities and trade unions all play roles in campaigning for legal change on behalf of their members or the communities they represent. Pressure groups such as Liberty (civil liberties) or Amnesty International focus sustained public and political pressure on specific legal issues. Trade unions have historically campaigned for employment law reform, winning protections including the national minimum wage, health and safety regulations, and equal pay legislation. Charities working in areas such as disability rights or children’s welfare often use legal challenges, published research and parliamentary lobbying to argue for law reform. These organisations provide ordinary citizens with collective voice that would be difficult to achieve individually.
exam_tip_html: Questions about citizens in the legal system often ask students to describe or explain specific roles — juror, magistrate, special constable. A common error is to confuse the roles: remember that a juror decides the verdict in Crown Court trials; a magistrate is a volunteer JP who decides the outcome in the vast majority (about 95%) of criminal cases in the magistrates’ court; and a special constable is a volunteer police officer with full powers. For an 8-mark Discuss question about how citizens can bring about change in the legal system, use connectives and present contrasting viewpoints — for example, the effectiveness of individual action (petition, legal challenge) versus collective action (pressure groups, trade unions). Name at least one real-world example, such as the Hillsborough campaign or the Stephen Lawrence case. For a 12-mark Evaluate, your conclusion must weigh the evidence — for instance, judging whether formal roles within the system (jury, magistrate) or external pressure (campaigning, lobbying) are more effective at bringing about change, and why. A phrase like “it depends” alone will not access the top band — add the criteria that determine which approach is more effective.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Citizens participate in the legal system in several formal roles: jurors decide verdicts in Crown Court trials; magistrates (Justices of the Peace) are unpaid volunteers who hear around 95% of criminal cases; special constables are volunteer police officers with full powers; tribunal lay members bring specialist knowledge to dispute resolution.
  • Police and Crime Commissioners are directly elected officials who hold local police forces to account and set policing priorities — a relatively recent (2012) form of democratic accountability in policing.
  • Citizens can work to change laws they believe are unjust through petitions, lobbying, demonstrations, media campaigns, legal challenges and collective action through pressure groups, trade unions and charities. Historical campaigns such as those of the Hillsborough families and the family of Stephen Lawrence demonstrate the impact citizens can have on legal reform.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a magistrate?
A) A legally trained judge who presides over Crown Court trials
B) An unpaid citizen volunteer who decides cases in the magistrates' court
C) An elected official who sets local policing priorities
D) A citizen selected at random to decide the verdict in a Crown Court trial
practice_questions.marks: B) An unpaid citizen volunteer who decides cases in the magistrates' court [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one difference between the role of a juror and the role of a magistrate.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. A full statement of one clear difference scores 2 marks (1 mark for identifying the difference, 1 mark for development or accurate specificity). Acceptable differences include: jurors are selected randomly and serve in the Crown Court, whereas magistrates are volunteers who apply and are appointed to the magistrates' court; jurors decide the verdict in serious criminal trials, while magistrates hear and decide approximately 95% of criminal cases; jurors are guided by a judge on points of law, while magistrates are advised by a legally qualified court adviser. A vague or incomplete statement scores 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which citizens can take action to bring about change in the legal system.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 mark for identifying the method, 1 mark for a developed description). Acceptable methods: joining or forming a pressure group to campaign for law reform; signing or organising a petition; lobbying MPs, councillors or government departments; participating in or organising a peaceful demonstration; using the media to publicise an injustice; bringing a legal challenge such as a judicial review; joining a trade union that campaigns for employment law reform. A one-line statement without development scores 1 mark per point.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A report by the fictional Centre for Civic Justice (2024) found that magistrates' courts in England and Wales dealt with 1.7 million criminal cases in 2023, compared with 93,000 Crown Court trials. The report noted that while magistrates are unpaid volunteers with no legal qualifications, their conviction rate for cases they hear is broadly comparable to that of Crown Court juries. The report argued that the magistracy represents a cost-effective way of delivering justice at scale, but warned that recruiting magistrates who reflect the diversity of local communities remains a significant challenge."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what this source tells us about the role of magistrates in the criminal justice system.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (magistrates handle the vast majority of criminal cases — 1.7 million compared with 93,000 Crown Court trials); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (magistrates are central to the functioning of the criminal justice system at scale, not a minor supplement to professional judges); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. explaining the role of the court adviser in guiding magistrates on law, or the range of sentences available to magistrates compared to Crown Court judges); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that goes beyond the source (e.g. noting the report's limitation — one organisation's data — or weighing the cost-effectiveness argument against the concern about diversity and the risk that a non-diverse bench may not reflect community perspectives). Pure summary scores no more than 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: A community group is considering which method of action to take to campaign for changes to sentencing law in their area. They are deciding between organising a petition and joining an established national pressure group. Discuss whether citizens working through established organisations are more effective at changing the law than taking individual or small-group action.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A well-developed discussion with contrasting viewpoints, connectives and at least one named real-world example on each side. Arguments for collective/organisational action: established organisations (pressure groups, trade unions, charities) have professional staff, legal expertise, media contacts and sustained public profile that individual action cannot match; campaigns by Liberty (civil liberties), Amnesty International (human rights) or trade unions for employment law have achieved legislative change; the Hillsborough families campaign gained greater impact through collective sustained effort. Arguments for individual/small-group action: grassroots campaigns can set the agenda that larger organisations later adopt; petitions can quickly gather large numbers of signatories; social media has reduced the cost of organising without a formal structure; individual legal challenges (judicial review) have directly changed government policy. A substantiated overall view is reached.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both viewpoints present, at least one named example, generally accurate. Conclusion present but may lack full substantiation.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on one or both sides but limited development or no named example.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about campaigning with little or no real-world reference.

practice_questions.text:
"The most important way citizens can participate in the legal system is by serving as jurors or magistrates rather than by campaigning to change the law."

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Sustained two-sided evaluation. Arguments in support: formal roles within the system (jury, magistrate, special constable, tribunal lay member) are constitutionally significant, with jurors deciding guilt or innocence in the most serious cases and magistrates handling approximately 95% of criminal cases; these roles ensure democratic participation in the delivery of justice; without citizens in these roles the system could not function. Arguments against: formal roles operate within existing law and cannot change it; campaigning for legal reform has a longer-term impact on the system itself — the Hillsborough families campaign led to changes in inquest law and police accountability; the Stephen Lawrence campaign led to the Macpherson Report and race relations law reform; trade union campaigning secured employment protections that shaped the law for millions of workers; in a democracy, the ability to change law may be more fundamental than administering existing law. Named examples used on both sides. Conclusion reaches a substantiated judgement — e.g. that formal roles are essential for day-to-day justice delivery while campaign action shapes what the law is; both matter, but their importance depends on whether the question is about administering the law as it stands or improving it.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example, conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking named examples.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of one or two roles with little evaluation.

glossary_terms.definition: A member of a jury: a group of twelve citizens selected at random to decide whether a defendant is guilty or not guilty in Crown Court trials.
A person who gives evidence in a legal proceeding, either because they observed the relevant events or because they have relevant expert knowledge.
A volunteer member of the public, also called a Justice of the Peace (JP), who sits on a magistrates' court bench to hear and decide less serious criminal cases.
A volunteer police officer who has the same powers as a regular (warranted) police officer but works on a part-time, unpaid basis.
An elected official responsible for a police force area, setting the local police and crime plan and holding the chief constable to account.
A specialist judicial body that resolves disputes in a specific area of law, such as employment or immigration, often with a legally qualified judge and lay members.
The criminal offence of giving false testimony under oath in a legal proceeding.
